locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; 40ft on a side loader, or a crane truck where a Rocky back yard has no run-up
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Rockhampton and Central Queensland. Honest advice on the Fitzroy, black soil, heat and Bowen Basin work.
locations.line: Rockhampton is a long way north of our Forest Hill yard, and pretending otherwise helps nobody. Most Rocky orders get filled out of Central Queensland stock rather than trucked eleven hundred kilometres, which is quicker and better for you. The trade-off is that what sits closest is not always the exact grade you had in mind, so the conversation is about matching what is available to what the job needs.
locations.uses: mining and drilling contractors kitting out for Bowen Basin work, cattle station gear, fencing and water fittings on the grazing country west of town, tool and plant storage for the trades, hay and feed on the smaller blocks along the river flats, machinery parts for the workshops and engineering shops, storage lifted clear of ground that has had the Fitzroy through it before, and site sheds and secure lockups on civil jobs
access:
The first thing about Rockhampton is the distance. A container coming from South East Queensland is the better part of two days of driving before anyone touches it, so we source locally when the stock is there, and when it is not we tell you it is coming a long way rather than quietly missing a date. Consolidating with other freight heading the same direction is often what makes an out-of-town order sensible, and that is a timing conversation more than anything else.

On the ground, Rocky splits fairly cleanly. The older suburbs on the north and south sides have generous street frontages and reasonable side access by city standards, and a tilt-tray with a 20ft on it will usually place a unit without needing anything clever. The newer estates on the fringes have narrower streets, tighter courts and cars parked on both sides, and that is where a delivery goes from routine to needing a plan. Out toward Gracemere and west, blocks get bigger, entries get longer, and the constraints stop being about width and start being about surface.

The soil is the other half of it. A lot of the country around Rockhampton is heavy black cracking clay. In the dry it splits open into fissures you can lose a boot in and it carries weight beautifully. After decent rain it turns to grease, and a loaded truck will either sink or slide, usually both. This is not a Rockhampton problem so much as a Central Queensland one, and the answer is always the same: wait for it to dry, or place the unit on the nearest hardstand and shift it across later.

Heat matters too, more than people expect. Through summer the middle of the day is genuinely dangerous for anyone standing on steel, and delivery crews start early and finish early for good reason. Storm season brings the same short, violent downpours that shut down black soil access, so a firm date through December to March is worth less than a date with some flexibility built into it.

sections.h: The Fitzroy, the flood line and what a container will not do
p: Rockhampton floods. Not occasionally and not gently, and anyone who has lived here through a big Fitzroy event knows the water comes up slowly, sits, and takes its time going away. It is worth being blunt about what a shipping container does and does not do in that situation. A container keeps rain off from above and it is a very good lockup. It is not a sealed vessel. Floodwater finds the door seals and comes in, and an empty container is buoyant enough that rising water will lift it and move it. Anyone telling you otherwise is selling you something.

What actually protects your contents is height. If the container sits above the level the water has historically reached on your block, the things inside it stay dry. That is the whole trick, and it is why placement on a Rockhampton property is a longer conversation than placement almost anywhere else. Local knowledge of what your street did in the big years beats any general rule we could give you. Bring that to the phone call and we will work the placement around it, including whether a unit on properly built-up ground or on blocks makes sense for you.

sections.h: Black steel in a Capricornia summer
p: A closed steel box sitting in full Rockhampton sun gets very hot, and the inside temperature runs well above the shade temperature outside for most of the afternoon. That is fine for steel, fencing, drums, tools and most machinery parts. It is not fine for anything with a battery, an adhesive, a rubber seal, a label, a plastic housing or a liquid that expands. Paint goes off. Aerosols are a genuinely bad idea. Electronics age fast.

There are practical fixes and they are worth doing at the start rather than after the first summer. Extra vents let hot air out of the top and pull cooler air in at the bottom. A lighter roof colour helps. Keeping the unit off bare ground with an air gap under it helps more than most people expect. If the container is going to hold something that genuinely cannot cook, say so before you buy and we will talk through insulation and ventilation options rather than let you find out in January.

sections.h: Kitting out for the Bowen Basin from a Rocky base
p: A lot of what gets bought here does not stay here. Rockhampton is a supply and staging town for coal and gas work out west, and containers get used accordingly: as secure stores for tooling and consumables that will be trucked to a camp, as workshop annexes at contractors' yards, and as the thing that holds the gear between one contract and the next. That use pattern changes what matters at purchase. Corner castings and a straight frame matter far more than cosmetic condition, because a unit that will be lifted onto a truck repeatedly needs to keep picking up cleanly. Doors that seal and swing without a fight matter, because someone will be opening them in the dark with dust in the hinges.

faqs.q: Will a container keep floodwater out on a Fitzroy River block?
faqs.a: No, and we will not tell you it does. A container is very good at keeping rain off from above, but floodwater reaches the door seals and gets in, and an empty unit will float and shift once the water is deep enough. What protects your contents in Rockhampton is height. Put the unit above the level the water has historically reached on your block and what is inside stays dry. Placement is the decision that matters here, and it is worth working out properly before delivery day rather than after.

faqs.q: Do containers for Rockhampton come from your Forest Hill yard, or from closer?
faqs.a: Usually from closer. Forest Hill is in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane, and trucking a box the whole way north makes a container more expensive and slower than it needs to be. Where Central Queensland stock matches what you are after, that is what we supply, and it can be inspected at the depot by arrangement. Where the spec is unusual, or the grade you need is not sitting in the region, it comes up from the south and we tell you that up front so the timing is not a surprise.

faqs.q: How hot does it get inside a container through a Rockhampton summer?
faqs.a: Hot enough that it changes what you should store in it. A sealed steel box in full Capricornia sun runs well above the outside shade temperature through the afternoon, and it holds that heat into the evening. Steel, fencing, drums, tools and parts do not care. Batteries, aerosols, paint, adhesives, electronics and anything with rubber seals do. Extra vents, a lighter roof and an air gap under the unit all help. Tell us what is going in before you buy and we will talk through ventilation rather than let you find out the hard way.

faqs.q: Which grade of container stands up best to Central Queensland heat and dust?
faqs.a: For anything that has to stay dry, a cargo-worthy unit is the sensible floor, and every cargo-worthy container is checked wind and watertight before it leaves. Newer one-trip units hold their coating longer and seal better if the contents warrant it. As-is units are cheap for a reason and are not sold as watertight, so they suit a laydown yard, a workshop screen or gear that does not mind weather. Out here the details that age worst are seals and hinges, because dust gets into everything, so look at how the doors move before you look at the paint.

locations.leadTime: Usually five to eight business days, and worth booking further out around a shutdown
locations.truck: Side loader for 40ft into a laydown yard; tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck where a unit has to go over a fence line
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Gladstone. Industrial site storage, shutdown season, harbour air and honest advice on lead times and access.
locations.line: Gladstone is an industrial town and it buys containers like one. Most enquiries here are about site storage, laydown yards and secure lockups on a project, not a box in a back yard. The easy part is access, because industrial estates are built for trucks. The hard part is timing, because demand here moves in waves and the wave everyone forgets about is shutdown season.
locations.uses: site storage and secure lockups on refinery, port and construction projects, tool stores and consumable cribs for maintenance contractors, laydown yard storage during shutdowns, workshop overflow at engineering and fabrication shops, marine and dive gear near the harbour, spare parts on rural blocks out toward Calliope and Miriam Vale, and general trade storage for the electricians, riggers and boilermakers who work the plants
access:
Delivery into Gladstone's industrial areas is about as straightforward as it gets. The estates around the port and the industrial precincts have wide roads, big turning circles and hardstand that will hold a loaded rigid without argument. A side loader with a 40ft on it works comfortably in that environment, and most yards can take a unit placed exactly where it is wanted rather than approximately.

The complications are site rules rather than terrain. Controlled industrial sites have their own induction, escort and permit requirements, and a truck that turns up without the paperwork sorted sits at the gate. That is not a delivery problem, it is a scheduling problem, and it is solved by knowing before the truck leaves who signs the driver in, what the site needs to see, and what hours the gate actually accepts deliveries. We would rather ask those questions a week out than have a driver on the phone at a boom gate.

Residential Gladstone is a different exercise. The older suburbs climb, and some of the streets on the hills are steep enough that a tilt-tray needs the right approach angle to unload without grounding. Newer estates on the flatter ground out toward Kirkwood and Calliope are easier, though the usual new-estate issues apply: narrow carriageways, parked trades utes, soft verges and a kerb the truck should not be putting a wheel over.

Out of town the country toward Miriam Vale and Agnes Water turns sandy and drains fast, which is good news after rain but means loose surfaces on any slope. Closer to the coast, salt is the constant, and it is the reason we push people here toward a better grade of unit than they would need inland.

sections.h: Shutdown season, and why storage gets scarce in a hurry
p: Gladstone's demand for storage is not steady. When a plant goes into a major maintenance shutdown, several hundred extra people arrive with tooling, spares, consumables and safety gear that all has to live somewhere secure for a few weeks or a few months. Every contractor on that job needs the same thing at the same time, and they all start ringing around at roughly the same moment. That is when availability tightens, and it is entirely predictable if you are the one planning the job.

The practical advice is simple. If you know a shutdown window, talk to us while it is still a date on a schedule rather than a week out. Locking units in early costs nothing and it means the gear arrives with somewhere to go. It also means we can plan how the units get here, because getting several containers to Gladstone at once is a freight exercise, and freight that is planned moves better and cheaper than freight that is urgent.

sections.h: What harbour air does to steel over the long run
p: Gladstone sits on a working harbour, and containers here live in salt-laden air permanently. Marine-grade corten steel handles that far better than ordinary mild steel does, which is the whole point of how these things are built, but the coating still does the real work and the coating is what degrades. Units that spend years here develop surface rust at the door frames, the roof seams and any spot where the paint has been cut or scraped.

None of that is dramatic if it is dealt with. Wire brushing and touching up a scrape when you notice it is a five-minute job that saves a fifteen-year problem. Keeping the unit off the ground so air moves under the floor stops the underside staying wet after rain. Greasing the door gear once or twice a year keeps the seals doing their job, and seals are what stand between your contents and a downpour. If the unit is going to sit near the water and hold anything worth protecting, buy a grade that starts in good condition rather than one you plan to fix.

sections.h: Getting a unit inside an industrial gate
p: The questions we ask before a Gladstone site delivery are not the same as the ones we ask a homeowner. Where does the truck report. Who inducts the driver. What PPE does the site expect at the gate. Is there a hold point on lifts. Are there overhead services across the yard. What is the surface where the container lands, and is it rated for the point loads under the corner castings. Is anything going to be stacked on this unit later, because that changes what the base has to be. None of these are difficult, but every one of them stops a truck cold if it is discovered at the gate rather than a week earlier. The surface question is the one that catches people most often on a working site. Made ground and crusher dust look identical to hardstand until a fully loaded container puts its whole weight through four corner castings, and then one corner keeps going. Where the base is not certain, the fix is timber bearers or concrete pads spreading the load, and it is far easier to put them down before the unit arrives than to lift it again afterwards. The same applies to anything running underneath the drop point. Site services, drainage and conduit are rarely where the old drawing says they are, and a container is not something you want to shift twice.

faqs.q: Can you get containers to Gladstone in time for a shutdown?
faqs.a: Usually, if we hear about it before it becomes urgent. Shutdown demand is spiky and predictable at the same time, because everyone on the job needs storage in the same fortnight. Give us the window while it is still a date on a schedule and we can source and freight the units in an orderly way, including grouping several onto the same run north. A week out, in the middle of the season, options narrow to whatever happens to be sitting in the region. The planning is what makes it work, not the panic.

faqs.q: Is it better to hire a container for a Gladstone shutdown than buy one?
faqs.a: For a defined project window, hire is usually the right call. You pay for the period you need it, the unit goes back at the end, and there is no asset sitting in a yard between contracts. Buying makes more sense when the container becomes permanent infrastructure at your own yard, when you want to modify it, or when the job keeps extending. If you genuinely cannot tell which it will be, start on hire and talk to us about what applying the hire toward a purchase would look like.

faqs.q: Can you deliver a container to Curtis Island?
faqs.a: Not by road, because there is no road. Anything crossing to the island moves through the site operators' own barge and logistics arrangements, and those are controlled by whoever holds that contract, not by us. What we can do is get the unit to a mainland laydown yard in good order and on time, ready for that crossing to be arranged at your end. Ring us with the timing and where it needs to land and we will work back from that.

faqs.q: Can containers be stacked in a laydown yard?
faqs.a: Physically yes, that is what they are designed for, but it depends on the units and the base. Stacking loads goes through the corner castings, so the castings and the frame have to be sound and the units have to be locked together properly with twistlocks. The ground underneath has to be level and able to carry the point loads, which is a real consideration on made ground. As-is units are not the ones to stack. Your site will also have its own lift and stacking rules, and those govern. Tell us stacking is the plan before you choose the units.

locations.depot: North Queensland depot stock where we can match it, otherwise a long run north from the Lockyer Valley
locations.leadTime: Around one to two weeks, and longer through the middle of the wet
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; side loader for 40ft where there is length to work with, which cane country generally has
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Mackay and the Pioneer Valley. Cane farm access, wet season timing, mining services and honest lead times.
locations.line: Mackay sits a long way north of us and the honest answer is that we source close to the job wherever the stock allows. What Mackay has in its favour is space. Cane country, mining service yards and Pioneer Valley farms all have room to land a container properly. What it does not have in its favour is the wet, and that is worth planning around.
locations.uses: spares, tooling and consumables for the mining services businesses that supply the Bowen Basin, workshop overflow at the engineering and fabrication yards, chemical drums, irrigation fittings and spare parts on cane farms through the Pioneer Valley, harvester and haul-out components between seasons, fodder and gear on the cattle blocks inland, secure trade storage in town, and dry storage on blocks where the shed is already full
access:
Cane country is generally kind to a delivery truck and occasionally treacherous, and the difference is entirely down to the last two hundred metres. Farm tracks and headlands are built for tractors and haul-outs, not for a loaded rigid, and they are often narrow, crowned, soft at the edges and bordered by a drain you cannot see under the grass. A headland that a tractor crosses without thinking will carry a truck in September and will not in February. Where the container is going onto a farm, the useful question is not whether the track exists but what it is made of and when it last had water on it.

The Pioneer Valley adds gradient. Once you head up toward Marian, Mirani and further in, the road narrows, the shoulders drop away and the driveways get steeper and shorter. Cane rail crossings appear where you do not expect them. Overhanging trees along the older valley roads clip anything with height on the deck, which matters for a high cube on a tilt-tray more than people realise. We would rather know about a low branch before the truck is committed than deal with it on the day.

In town, Mackay is straightforward by city standards. The industrial estates around Paget are built for exactly this kind of work, with hardstand, wide access and yards used to trucks. Residential areas are a mixed bag, with the older suburbs offering reasonable frontage and the newer northern estates presenting the usual narrow-street, soft-verge problem.

The wet season governs everything. From about December through March, and sometimes later, the district gets rainfall in quantities that make southern rain look like a rumour. Ground that carried a truck last week will not this week. Creeks come up fast and go down fast. We do not fight that. We move the date, and locals do not find that surprising.

sections.h: Headlands, drains and a truck that has to turn around
p: The single most common thing that turns a straightforward cane farm delivery into an awkward one is not getting in, it is getting out. A rigid with a side loader needs somewhere to turn or somewhere to reverse a long way, and a headland with a drain on one side and a block of standing cane on the other offers neither. It is worth walking the route before delivery day with the truck in mind rather than the tractor, checking the width at the tightest point, what the surface does when it is wet, and where the vehicle can turn around once the container is off.

The other thing worth thinking through is where the doors end up facing. On a farm the container usually gets loaded from a ute or a tractor with a forklift on the back, and the approach to it is set by the shape of the headland. Doors facing the wrong way means every load-in becomes a three-point turn. It costs nothing to decide this before the unit is placed and it is a genuine nuisance to change afterwards.

sections.h: Three months of rain, and what it does to a delivery calendar
p: Mackay's wet season is not a southern wet season with the volume turned up. It is a different category of weather, and it reshapes what is possible for months at a time. Unsealed tracks stop carrying weight. Low crossings go under. Ground that looked solid on inspection turns to a surface that a loaded truck will cut half a metre of rut into. There is no clever equipment answer to that.

So the way we handle Mackay through the wet is to build slack into the date rather than promise a morning. If the country is right, the delivery happens. If forty millimetres landed on your place overnight, it moves, and it moves by a few days rather than a few weeks. Planning a delivery for the drier months when the timing is flexible is simply the easier path, and anyone who has farmed here for a season already knows that.

sections.h: Supplying the Basin from a Mackay yard
p: A large share of Mackay's container demand comes from businesses that service coal operations inland rather than from the mines themselves. Fabrication shops, hydraulic specialists, labour hire outfits, tyre and undercarriage businesses, and maintenance contractors all carry inventory that has to be secure, findable and out of the weather, and they all run out of shed space before they run out of work. A container in the yard is the cheap answer to that, and often several of them lined up become the de facto store. Where that is the use, buy for the frame rather than the finish. These units get shifted between yards, loaded with heavy awkward things, opened in the rain and closed by someone in a hurry. Straight rails, sound corner castings, doors that swing true and seals in good order are what makes a unit still useful in a decade. Paint is cosmetic. Ask for photos of the actual unit on request before delivery if you want to see exactly what is coming.

faqs.q: Can you deliver a container onto a cane farm headland?
faqs.a: Often yes, and the deciding factor is the surface rather than the width. Headlands are built for tractors and haul-outs, and a loaded truck is a different proposition, particularly near a drain edge or on ground that has had rain on it. What we need to know beforehand is the narrowest point on the track, what the surface is made of, whether there is anywhere to turn around once the unit is off, and what the weather has done on your place recently. Where the headland will not carry a truck, the usual answer is to place the unit on firmer ground nearby.

faqs.q: What happens to a Mackay delivery during the wet season?
faqs.a: It gets scheduled with room in it. From around December through March the district gets rainfall that will stop a loaded truck getting into places it managed easily a fortnight earlier, and low crossings can be out for a day or two at a time. We do not try to force a delivery through that, because the result is a bogged truck and ruts in your track that last a year. We move the date, usually by a few days. If the timing is genuinely fixed, the alternative is placing the unit on hardstand and shifting it once things dry out.

faqs.q: Does Mackay humidity cause sweating inside a container?
faqs.a: It can, and it is worth designing around rather than discovering. Warm humid air gets into a container during the day, then the steel roof cools overnight and the moisture in that air condenses on the underside and drips. The contents get wet without a drop of rain coming through anything. Extra vents make a real difference, keeping the unit up off the ground helps air move under it, and putting things in dry is the biggest single factor. Do not load damp canvas, green timber or wet gear into a closed box up here.

faqs.q: Where does stock for a Mackay order actually come from?
faqs.a: Wherever it makes sense for your job. Our own yard is at Forest Hill in the Lockyer Valley, which is a long way south of Mackay, so for northern orders we look first at depot stock closer to you. That is faster and it keeps freight sensible. Units at those depots can be inspected by arrangement. If the grade, size or spec you want is not in the north, it comes up from the south, and grouping it with other freight heading the same way is often what makes the timing and the cost work. We will tell you which it is.

locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Townsville. Dry tropics ground, cyclone season, port and defence work, plus honest lead times from the south.
locations.line: Townsville is a long haul from the Lockyer Valley, so we work from northern stock where the grade and size line up, and say plainly when a unit has to come up from the south. What makes Townsville interesting is the ground rather than the trucking. The dry tropics bake to a surface that holds anything for eight months, then one storm turns it to slop.
locations.uses: secure storage for defence contractors and the trades that service them, tool and plant stores for civil and construction crews, spares and consumables at the port and marine services businesses, cattle and fencing gear on the grazing country inland toward Charters Towers, cane and machinery storage down in the Burdekin, chemical and fertiliser lockups, workshop overflow in the industrial estates, and cyclone-season storage for people clearing a yard before the season starts
access:
The defining feature of delivering here is what the dry tropics do to ground. For most of the year the surface bakes to something close to concrete, cracks open, and will carry a fully loaded truck across a paddock without a mark. Then the build-up arrives, a storm drops a serious amount of rain in an hour, and the same surface turns to slop that a rigid will sink into to the axles. There is very little middle ground. The practical consequence is that a Townsville delivery in October is a different job to the same delivery in February, on the same block, with the same truck.

In the city itself, access is generally good. The industrial estates are laid out with trucks in mind, the arterials are wide, and the flatter northern and western suburbs present few problems for a tilt-tray. The trickier deliveries are around the older suburbs on the slopes near the hill, where streets narrow, driveways are short and steep, and the frontages were laid out long before anyone was reversing a rigid down them. Overhead power in the older streets sits lower than in newer estates, which matters when a container is going up on a tilt deck.

Out of town the country opens up quickly. Blocks toward Woodstock, Giru and the Burdekin have space and long entries, and the constraint moves back to surface and to gates. Grids, culverts and single-lane bridges on rural access roads are worth mentioning before delivery day, because a grid rated for a tractor is not necessarily rated for a loaded rigid, and finding that out with a container on the back is nobody's idea of a good afternoon.

Salt is a constant near the water and dust is a constant everywhere else, and between them they are hard on door seals and hinges. That is the part of a container that fails first up here, not the walls.

sections.h: Ground that bakes hard, then turns to slop
p: People who have not lived in the dry tropics assume the wet season is the only rain risk. In practice it is the build-up storms that catch deliveries out, because they are localised, violent and over in an hour. Your street can get eighty millimetres while the airport records nothing. This is why we ask what the weather has actually done on your block rather than what the forecast said for the city, and why we would rather ring you the day before than send a truck into a paddock on someone's optimism.

For placement, the flip side of hard-baking ground is that it moves. Cracking clay opens up in the dry and swells shut in the wet, which means a container that was dead level in September can be sitting on three corners by March. It is not a disaster, but it puts the frame in a twist and doors that closed easily start to bind. Setting the unit on properly bedded blocks or a compacted pad, with the load spread under the corner castings, is what stops that. Check it after the first wet and pack it up if it has moved.

sections.h: Cyclone season, tie-downs and honest expectations
p: An empty shipping container is a large steel sail and it weighs a lot less than people assume. In a serious wind event, an empty or lightly loaded unit can be moved, and it does not need to travel far to do damage. A loaded container is a very different proposition, but loaded is not a plan, it is a condition that happens to be true today. If a container is going to live on a site through cyclone season, the sensible approach is to think about how it is restrained and where it sits relative to things you care about, and to talk to an engineer if it is on a commercial site with obligations attached.

The same season brings the flooding question, and the answer is the same one we give everywhere. A container keeps rain out from above. It is not sealed against rising water, floodwater reaches the door seals and gets in, and an empty unit will float. The thing that keeps your contents dry is having the unit above where water has historically reached on your block. Placement solves this. The steel does not.

sections.h: Port, garrison and the trades in between
p: Townsville's container demand is unusually broad because the economy is. There is a working port, a large defence presence with a long tail of contractors around it, a heavy civil and construction sector, agriculture on both sides of the city, and a marine services industry. What they have in common is a need for lockable, relocatable storage that does not require a development approval to put in a yard and can be sold or moved when the contract ends. For that pattern of use, buy for the mechanicals. Corner castings that are true, a frame with no twist in it, and doors that seal and swing properly are what makes a unit still worth owning after several relocations. Cosmetic rust on a panel is a paint problem. A racked frame is a permanent one. If you want to see exactly what is coming, ask for photos of the specific unit on request before delivery and we will send them.

faqs.q: Do I need to tie a container down for cyclone season in Townsville?
faqs.a: It is worth thinking about seriously, particularly for an empty or lightly loaded unit. An empty container presents a large flat side to the wind and weighs far less than its size suggests, so it can be moved in a severe event. A well-loaded unit is much harder to shift, but you cannot rely on it staying loaded. Where it sits matters as much as any restraint: clear of what you would not want it hitting, and not somewhere it will become a problem for a neighbour. On a commercial site with obligations, get engineering advice rather than ours.

faqs.q: The ground on my Townsville block is rock hard. Is that good enough to sit a container on?
faqs.a: Usually yes for delivery, but not necessarily for the long term. Dry tropics clay bakes to something close to concrete and will carry the truck easily, then it swells and softens through the wet and the container settles unevenly. A unit sitting on three corners twists the frame and the doors start to bind. The fix is cheap and worth doing at the start: bed the unit on blocks or a compacted pad with the load spread under the corner castings, then check and re-pack it after the first proper wet.

faqs.q: Can I inspect a container in Townsville, or only at your Forest Hill yard?
faqs.a: Both are possible. Our own yard is at Forest Hill in the Lockyer Valley and anyone is welcome there during business hours if they ring first. For northern orders the unit usually sits at a depot much closer to you, and those inspections are by arrangement rather than drop-in, because the depots are working yards with their own access rules. Ring us, tell us when you can get there, and we will organise it. If you cannot get to a yard at all, we can send photos of the actual unit on request before delivery.

faqs.q: How long does a Townsville delivery take to organise?
faqs.a: Generally one to two weeks, and the variable is where the right unit starts from. If northern depot stock matches what you need, it is at the shorter end. If the size, grade or spec has to come up from South East Queensland, it is at the longer end, and grouping it with other freight heading north is usually what makes that sensible. Through the wet, add room to the date. We would rather quote you a realistic window than a good-sounding one we have to walk back.

locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; 40ft on a side loader where there is room; crane truck for tight coastal and hillside blocks
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Cairns and the Far North. Wet tropics humidity, corrosion, range road access and realistic wet season timing.
locations.line: Cairns is the furthest north we deliver regularly, and stock comes from a Far North depot wherever the grade allows, because trucking a box two thousand kilometres serves nobody. The bigger issue up here is not distance, it is climate. The wet tropics are hard on steel, hard on what is stored in it, and for months a year they decide when a truck reaches an unsealed block.
locations.uses: gear storage for reef and rainforest tourism operators between seasons, dive and marine equipment near the inlet, tool and plant storage for the trades, fertiliser, chemical and machinery parts on cane and tropical fruit farms, secure storage for accommodation and hospitality businesses, workshop overflow in the industrial estates, and dry storage on Tablelands blocks where the shed filled up years ago
access:
Cairns is a narrow city. The coastal strip between the range and the sea is not wide, and a lot of the residential area is packed into it, which means blocks are tighter and side access scarcer than the population would suggest. In the older suburbs the streets are close, the vegetation is aggressive and overhanging, and a tilt-tray needs more clear height than people expect once the deck is up. In the northern beaches the ground turns sandy and soft close to the shoreline, and the good-looking level lawn is often the least load-bearing part of the property.

Going inland the terrain changes fast. The Tablelands sit several hundred metres above the coast and the range roads that get you there are steep, tightly wound and in places narrow enough that a long vehicle is a genuine consideration rather than a formality. Roadworks and slips on those roads are a fact of life in the wet. A container going to Mareeba, Atherton or beyond is a different day's work to one going to a flat block near the highway, and it gets planned as such.

Then there is rainfall, which in this part of the country is not a weather event but a climate. Unsealed access roads and farm tracks in the wet tropics do not merely get muddy, they stop being roads. Creek crossings that are ankle deep in September are impassable in February, and some properties are genuinely cut off for days at a time. Nobody local finds this surprising. What it means for a delivery is that between roughly December and April, any address that is not on sealed road with hardstand at the end of it is a date we set with room in it and confirm the day before.

Humidity is the constant that never lets up. It is hard on hinges, hard on seals, and it is the reason units up here need looking after rather than ignoring.

sections.h: Rust, humidity and what actually survives up here
p: The wet tropics do to painted steel what a decade elsewhere does. Constant humidity, salt in the air near the coast, and rainfall in genuinely large quantities mean that any scratch through the coating starts working almost immediately. Corten steel is designed for this and it is why containers last as long as they do, but the coating is still the front line and the places it fails first are predictable: door frames, the roof seams, the underside of the floor rails, and anywhere something has been dragged against a panel.

The maintenance that keeps a unit good here is unglamorous and takes very little time. Touch up scrapes when you see them rather than at the end of the year. Grease the door gear and check the rubber seals, because a hardened seal in this climate lets water in during the first serious downpour. Keep the container up off the ground so air moves underneath and the floor rails are not sitting in a wet spot for months. Clear leaf litter off the roof, because organic matter holding moisture against paint is what actually eats it. On grade, this is the one part of the country where paying for a better unit up front usually pays for itself. Every cargo-worthy container is checked wind and watertight before it leaves, and that is the sensible minimum for anything that has to stay dry here. As-is units are not sold as watertight and up here that distinction is not academic, it is the difference between storage and a very large planter box.

sections.h: When the wet decides the date
p: Between about December and April, access is the schedule. Unsealed roads on the Tablelands and out through the cane and fruit country stop carrying loads. Creek crossings that were nothing become impassable. Some properties are cut off entirely for a few days at a stretch, and there is no truck and no driver that changes that. We plan Far North deliveries in the wet with flexible dates and a confirmation call the day before, and we tell people honestly that a fixed morning is not something we can promise into that country in February.

The upside is that the dry season here is superb for this work. From about May onward the roads firm up, the tracks carry weight, and a delivery that would have been a fortnight of watching the radar becomes routine. If your timing has any give in it at all, that is the window to use.

sections.h: The climb to the Tablelands
p: Getting a container up onto the Tablelands is its own exercise. The range roads climb hard, wind tightly, and have sections where a long vehicle needs the full width to make a bend. Slips, roadworks and single-lane sections are common enough in the wet that a route can change on the morning. None of that makes it impossible, and containers go up there regularly, but it does mean the delivery is a planned day rather than a slot, and it means we would rather talk through the exact address and the last few kilometres of approach before we commit to a date. Once you are on top, the country is easier: bigger blocks, longer entries, and volcanic red soil that drains well and carries a truck far better than the coastal ground below.

faqs.q: Can a container get up the range to Atherton or Mareeba?
faqs.a: Yes, and it goes regularly, but it is planned rather than squeezed in. The range roads are steep and tightly wound with sections where a long vehicle needs the full carriageway, and slips or roadworks can change the route on the morning. What we want to know beforehand is the exact address and what the last few kilometres look like, because that decides the truck. Once you are on the Tablelands the deliveries themselves are usually easier than on the coast, with more room and red soil that carries weight well.

faqs.q: Will unsealed roads stop a delivery in the Cairns wet season?
faqs.a: Sometimes, yes, and we would rather say so than pretend otherwise. Between roughly December and April, unsealed access in the wet tropics stops carrying loaded trucks, creek crossings go up, and some properties are genuinely cut off for days. We set dates in that period with room in them and confirm the day before. If the timing is fixed, the workable option is often to land the unit on sealed hardstand nearby and move it in once the road firms up.

faqs.q: How badly does the Cairns climate rust a container?
faqs.a: Faster than anywhere else we deliver, but it is manageable. Corten steel is built for weather and the walls are not what fails. It is the coating, and the spots that go first are the door frames, roof seams, floor rails and anywhere the paint has been scraped. Touch up scrapes when you notice them, grease the door gear, check the seals, keep leaf litter off the roof and keep the unit off the ground so air moves under it. Do that and it stays sound. Ignore it for a few wet seasons and it will show.

faqs.q: Do containers need extra vents in the Cairns climate?
faqs.a: In most cases up here, yes, and it is much cheaper to do at the start. Warm saturated air gets into the box during the day, the roof cools overnight, and the moisture condenses on the steel and drips onto whatever is underneath. That happens without a drop of rain getting in. Additional vents low and high let air move through and reduce it considerably. Raising the unit off the ground helps as well, and loading things dry helps most. Anything with paper, fabric, leather or electronics in it will thank you for the vents.

locations.name: Bundaberg
locations.depot: Loaded at the Lockyer Valley yard and run north up the Bruce, or brought across from Wide Bay depot stock
locations.leadTime: Usually three to five business days
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; side loader for 40ft, which suits farm entries and industrial yards here
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Bundaberg and the Burnett. Cane and small crop storage, sandy coastal soils, river flooding and real access advice.
locations.line: Bundaberg is the closest of our northern runs and the easiest to service properly. It is a straight trip up the Bruce, so lead times here look more like the south than like Cairns. What makes Bundy its own job is the ground: cane and small crop country inland with real substance to it, and sandy coastal blocks that lie about how much weight they will take.
locations.uses: chemical, fertiliser and irrigation fittings on the cane blocks, crates, bins and picking gear for the small crop and macadamia growers, tractor and implement spares, secure trade storage in town, boat and fishing gear on the coastal blocks, storage for gear that needs to sit above where the Burnett has reached before, tool stores on building sites, and general dry storage on rural blocks where the shed ran out of room a long time ago
access:
Bundaberg divides into three delivery environments and they behave completely differently. In town, the streets are generous by regional standards and most residential deliveries are a straightforward tilt-tray job, provided there is a clear run at the drop point and nothing overhead. The industrial areas are easy, with hardstand and room for a side loader to work a 40ft properly.

The farming country inland and to the south is the volume of the work. Cane blocks, small crop farms and macadamia country have long entries, wide gates and generally well-formed tracks, and a 40ft on a side loader fits into that world without drama. The catch is the same as anywhere with irrigation: soft edges where water has been running, headland drains hidden under grass, and low crossings on farm tracks that are fine in July and not in January. Harvest also puts a lot of slow, wide machinery on the district's roads, which does not stop a delivery but does affect what time of day it should happen.

Out toward Bargara, Moore Park and the coastal strip, the ground turns sandy. It looks firm, drains well after rain and generally carries a truck fine on a formed driveway, but off the formed surface it can be very soft indeed, and a rigid that puts a wheel onto a nice-looking lawn will find the sand underneath. The other coastal issue is the blocks themselves, which are often smaller, closer together and fenced tight, so getting a 20ft into a back yard sometimes means a lift rather than a slide.

The country closer to the river carries silt and heavier soils that hold water for days after decent rain, and that is where a delivery gets moved rather than forced.

sections.h: The Burnett, and what height actually buys you
p: Bundaberg has been through serious flooding and people here do not need a lecture about it. What is worth being clear about is the limit of what a shipping container does. It is an excellent lockup and it keeps rain off from above. It is not sealed against rising water. Floodwater reaches the door seals and gets in, and an empty container has enough buoyancy that deep water will lift it and move it somewhere you did not choose.

What genuinely protects the things inside is elevation. A unit sitting above the level water has reached on your block keeps its contents dry, and that is the whole of the benefit. It makes placement the most important decision in the whole purchase for anyone on low ground here, and it is worth spending time on rather than putting the container where it happens to be convenient. Tell us what your block did in the bad years and we will work the placement around that, including whether it is worth sitting the unit up on blocks.

sections.h: Cane, small crops and a shed that filled up years ago
p: The Burnett grows a genuinely wide range of things, and that variety shows up in what people store. Cane blocks want somewhere secure and dry for chemical, drums, irrigation fittings, fencing and spare parts. Small crop and horticulture operations want crates, bins, netting, picking gear and packing supplies out of the weather and out of the way between seasons. Macadamia growers want somewhere for harvest gear that sits idle most of the year.

What all of that has in common is that it is seasonal, bulky, and worth money. A container handles it well and does not require a slab, an approval process or a builder. The one job it is poor at is bulk grain or bulk anything loose, because the side walls are corrugated sheet built for racking and torsion, not for tonnes of loose material pressing outward. Bagged, drummed, crated and palletised is what a container is for.

sections.h: Sand near the coast, heavy country inland
p: The soil difference between the coastal strip and the river country changes what has to go under the unit. On sand, the problem is not drainage, it is bearing: the surface is loose, it moves under a point load, and a container's weight goes almost entirely through four corner castings. Pads or bearers that spread that load across a wider footprint stop the corners burying themselves over the following year. On the heavier river soils the issue reverses and becomes drainage, because a unit sitting in a spot that stays wet will have its floor rails in water for days after rain, and that is where corrosion starts. Both problems have the same cheap answer, which is to decide what goes under the unit before it turns off the road rather than after it has settled. Concrete pads, heavy hardwood bearers or well-compacted road base under each corner spread the weight and keep the container out of standing water. Get it level at placement and check it again after the first proper wet, because a container that has gone out of square is not obvious to look at. What you notice is a door that used to close easily and now needs a shoulder, and by then the frame has already taken the twist.

faqs.q: Does putting a container on higher ground actually protect what is inside?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the only thing that does. A container is not sealed against rising water. Floodwater gets in at the door seals and an empty unit will float and move once water is deep enough, so the steel is not what protects your gear. Height is. A container placed above the level the Burnett has historically reached on your block keeps its contents dry, and that makes placement the most important decision in the purchase. Work it out from what your block actually did in the bad years, not from a general rule.

faqs.q: Is there a time of year that is harder for deliveries around Bundaberg?
faqs.a: Two things affect it. Through the summer storm months the heavier soils closer to the river hold water for days after rain, and a loaded truck on that ground will bog and cut ruts, so those dates get moved rather than forced. Then there is harvest, which puts a lot of slow and wide machinery on district roads. That does not stop a delivery, but it changes what time of day makes sense, and coordinating around it is easier if we know the farm is in the middle of a run.

faqs.q: Can a container be used for fertiliser and chemical storage on a farm?
faqs.a: Plenty are, and for drummed and bagged product in a locked, dry, shaded box it works well. Two things to get right. Ventilation, because a sealed steel box in Bundaberg summer heat builds temperature and fumes, and extra vents are worth fitting from the start. And segregation, because chemical storage carries real obligations around what can be stored with what, bunding and labelling, and those rules come from the product and your own requirements, not from us. Set it up properly and check what the labels require before you load it.

faqs.q: What should a container sit on in sandy coastal ground near Bargara?
faqs.a: Something that spreads the load. Sand drains beautifully and it looks solid, but almost the entire weight of a container goes down through four corner castings, and on loose sand those corners will work their way in over a season and put the frame out of level. Concrete pads, heavy timber bearers or well-compacted road base under each corner sorts it. Get it level at placement and check it after the first wet, because doors that bind are almost always a levelling problem rather than a door problem.

locations.name: Hervey Bay
locations.depot: Loaded at the Lockyer Valley yard and run north up the Bruce through Gympie and Maryborough
locations.leadTime: Usually three to five business days
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft on a normal block; crane truck where a unit has to go over a fence on a canal or beachside lot
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Hervey Bay. Advice on tight beachside blocks, canal frontages, sea air, caravan and boat storage and hire options.
locations.line: Hervey Bay is an easy run for us and a fiddly one to deliver into, and those two things are unrelated. The trip up the Bruce is short and so is the lead time. The difficulty is on the block: tidy, tightly planned lots, canal frontages, and yards that already hold a boat and a caravan. Getting the size right matters more here than anywhere on this list.
locations.uses: boat, tender and fishing gear on the waterfront blocks, caravan and camper accessories for people who travel half the year, furniture and household storage during a downsize or a renovation, tools and stock for the local trades, storage for the marine and charter businesses that work off the bay, overflow for holiday letting operators between seasons, and secure lockups on the acreage blocks out toward Burrum Heads and Howard
access:
The typical Hervey Bay residential block is level, tidy and not especially large, and that combination produces a very specific delivery problem. There is usually just enough room for a truck out front and not quite enough room to get a unit down the side. Fences here tend to be solid, side setbacks are narrow, and there is often an air conditioning unit, a rainwater tank or a garden bed exactly where the container needs to travel. That is why a good proportion of the deliveries in this town end up being a lift over the fence rather than a slide down the side, and why we ask about side access before we quote a truck rather than after.

Canal and waterfront properties add their own set of constraints. Frontages are frequently narrow, the street is often a cul de sac with limited room to manoeuvre a long vehicle, and the good hard ground stops at the property line. Retaining structures on canal edges are not something to be putting a loaded truck near without knowing what is under them. Where a crane lift is required, we need to know what is overhead, where the power runs, and whether there is a clear standing spot for the truck, and those are answerable questions on the phone.

The soils along the coastal strip are sandy and drain fast, which is helpful after rain and unhelpful under a corner casting. What looks like firm level lawn will take a wheel a surprising distance if the truck strays off the formed driveway. New driveways are the other recurring problem: a lot of housing here is recent, and green concrete or a decorative driveway is worth mentioning up front so the truck can be positioned somewhere else.

Out of town toward Burrum Heads, Torbanlea and Howard, blocks are bigger and the constraints revert to gates, grids and what the track is made of.

sections.h: Beachside blocks with nowhere to put a truck
p: The size conversation in Hervey Bay is worth having honestly before anything gets ordered. A 20ft is the default for a reason and it holds a genuinely useful amount, but on a lot of blocks here it takes up more of the yard than people picture, and it needs clear space in front of the doors as well as under the box. Doors on a standard unit swing wide and they need roughly the width of the container again in clear ground to open properly. Nobody wants to discover that with the container already down.

For a lot of households here a 10ft is the better answer. It fits behind a garage, it leaves the yard usable, and for storing camping gear, tools, fishing equipment and the accumulated contents of a shed it is plenty. The rule of thumb worth applying is to measure the space you actually have clear, subtract the door swing, and then decide, rather than choosing the size first and hoping.

sections.h: Vans, boats and the storage that comes with retiring here
p: A large share of the demand here comes from people who have moved to the bay, downsized the house and kept a lifestyle that requires equipment. Caravans, boats, kayaks, camping gear, fishing tackle, tools accumulated over a working life, and the furniture that did not fit into a smaller place. That is a slightly different storage problem to a farm or a work site: it is mostly domestic, it is mostly seasonal, and a fair bit of it is worth stealing.

Which makes the lock the part of the specification people underrate. A lockbox welded over the handle so bolt cutters cannot reach the shackle, doors that seal properly so nothing gets damp over a wet summer, and placement where the unit is visible from the house rather than hidden behind it are all worth more than a better paint job. If the container will be holding anything with fabric, leather, paper or electronics in it, add vents at the same time, because a closed steel box in coastal humidity will sweat overnight.

sections.h: Short hire for a move, a reno or a downsize
p: Not everyone needs to own one. A very common Hervey Bay situation is a few months of storage during a house move, a renovation, or the gap between selling one place and settling on another, and hire suits that exactly. The unit arrives, it sits in the driveway or on the block, it gets loaded at your own pace rather than a removalist's, and it goes away when it is no longer needed. There is no asset left over and no problem of what to do with it afterwards. Buying makes more sense once the storage need is permanent, or if you want to modify the unit, or when the hire period starts stretching past the point where owning would have been cheaper. If you are honestly unsure which one you are, start on hire and ring us when you know. We would rather adjust than sell you something that ends up sitting in the yard doing nothing.

faqs.q: Will a container fit on a standard Hervey Bay block and still leave room for the caravan?
faqs.a: Often, but it is worth measuring first rather than assuming. A 20ft takes more of a tidy suburban yard than people picture, and it needs clear ground in front of the doors as well, roughly another container width, so they can open fully. On a lot of blocks here a 10ft leaves the yard usable and still holds a shed's worth of gear. Work out the clear space you actually have, subtract the door swing and the van's parking spot, and choose the size from that.

faqs.q: Can I hire a container for a few months while I downsize?
faqs.a: Yes, and that is one of the most common reasons people ring us from Hervey Bay. Hire suits a defined period: a move, a renovation, or the gap between settlements. The unit turns up, you load it at your own pace instead of a removalist's clock, and it goes away when you are done, with no asset left over. If the period keeps extending or the storage need turns out to be permanent, ring us and we will talk about what moving to a purchase looks like.

faqs.q: Does the sea air at Hervey Bay wreck a container?
faqs.a: It does not wreck it, but it does mean the unit needs a small amount of attention rather than none. Containers are built from corten steel precisely because they spend their working lives at sea, so the steel itself is not the weak point. The coating is, and it gives way first at the door frames, roof seams and any scratch. Touch up scrapes when you see them, grease the door gear, check the seals once a year, and keep the unit off the ground so air moves under the floor rails. That is genuinely the whole maintenance list.

faqs.q: There is no way down the side of my house. What are the options?
faqs.a: This is common here and it does not stop the job. Where the side setback is too narrow or there is a tank, an air conditioner or a garden bed in the way, the unit goes over the fence on a crane truck instead of down the side on a tilt-tray. What we need to know first is what is overhead, particularly power lines and large trees, where the truck can stand on the street, and whether the neighbouring airspace is clear. Send us a couple of photos of the frontage and the drop point and we can usually tell you straight away.

locations.name: Maryborough
locations.depot: Loaded at the Lockyer Valley yard and run straight up the Bruce Highway
locations.leadTime: Usually three to five business days
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; side loader for 40ft into the industrial yards, where there is length to work with
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Maryborough. Mary River flooding, heritage streets, industrial and workshop storage, plus honest delivery advice.
locations.line: Maryborough gets treated as an afterthought to Hervey Bay and it should not be. It is a different town: older, built around a working river, with a real industrial and engineering base, and a street pattern laid out for horses rather than for a rigid with a container on the deck. It also floods, properly, and that shapes where things get put.
locations.uses: workshop and parts storage for the engineering, rail and fabrication businesses, tool stores for the building trades, machinery spares on the surrounding farms and timber blocks, dry storage for gear that needs to live above the Mary's flood level, secure storage on commercial premises in the older parts of town, hay and feed on the rural blocks out toward Tiaro and Bauple, and household storage during a renovation on one of the older houses
access:
Maryborough is an old town and it shows in the deliveries. The central streets are wide enough, but the older residential areas have narrow carriageways, mature street trees with low canopies, deep kerb and channel, and driveways cut for a car in the 1950s. Overhead clearance is the thing that catches people out, because a tilt-tray needs vertical room to angle the deck and a fig or a poinciana that has been there eighty years does not care about your delivery. It is worth looking up before delivery day, and it is worth telling us if there is a low branch, because the answer is often a different truck rather than a cancelled job.

The queenslanders that make up a lot of the older housing stock come with their own issue: high-set houses on stumps, steep short driveways up from the street, and no side access to speak of. On those blocks a container frequently ends up placed in the front third of the property rather than tucked away behind, simply because that is where the truck can reach, and that is a conversation worth having before rather than after.

Industrial Maryborough is the opposite and it is easy. The engineering and rail-related yards are set up for heavy vehicles, with hardstand, wide gates and room to place a 40ft exactly where it should go. Those deliveries are usually the simplest of the week.

Ground varies with proximity to the river. The flats carry alluvial silt and heavy soils that hold water for a good while after rain, and they will not take a loaded truck in the days following decent falls. Further out toward Tiaro and Bauple the country firms up and drains better. The general rule here is that the closer to the Mary you are, the more the recent weather governs the date.

sections.h: A river town with two levels
p: Maryborough's relationship with the Mary River is not theoretical. The lower parts of town have been under water more than once and the people who live there know exactly which streets go and in what order. So the useful thing we can offer is not reassurance but clarity about what a container does. It keeps rain out from above and it is a serious lockup. It is not a sealed vessel. Water rising from below reaches the door seals and comes in, and an empty container is buoyant enough to be lifted and carried off by deep water.

The protection is height, full stop. A unit sitting above the level the Mary has reached on your particular block will keep its contents dry, and that is why placement is the decision worth arguing about. On a property that has had water through it before, the right spot is often not the convenient spot. Tell us what your block did and how deep it got, and we will work out where the truck can reach that also puts the unit where you need it.

sections.h: Heritage streets, low canopies and short steep driveways
p: The character that makes Maryborough worth living in is exactly what makes it awkward to deliver into. Street trees planted a very long time ago hang low over narrow carriageways. Kerbs are deep. Driveways rise sharply from the street to a high-set house and then run out of room. A tilt-tray needs height and a run-up, and on a lot of these blocks it has neither.

None of that is a dead end, but it changes the plan. Sometimes it is a smaller unit. Sometimes it is a crane truck lifting over the fence line. Sometimes it is placing the container closer to the street than anybody would ideally like. What it always is, is a question best answered before the truck is loaded. A couple of photos of the frontage, the driveway and anything overhead tell us more than a paragraph of description ever will.

sections.h: Workshops, rail and the parts problem
p: Maryborough has a genuine engineering and manufacturing base, and that produces a very specific container demand: somewhere secure and dry for parts, jigs, tooling, offcuts and consumables that are too valuable to leave outside and too bulky to fit into a shed that filled up long ago. A container in the yard is the cheapest floor space anyone will ever buy, and it can be moved when the yard layout changes. For that use the specification is about the frame rather than the finish. Straight rails, true corner castings, doors that seal and swing without a fight, and a floor in sound condition are what makes a unit worth having in ten years. Where it is going to be lifted between sites, or stacked, the castings matter more again. Ask for photos of the specific unit on request before delivery if you want to see precisely what turns up rather than a stock image. Ventilation is worth a thought too, because this is a humid town and a sealed steel box holding tooling and steel stock will sweat overnight and put condensation onto everything in it. Extra vents cost very little at the outset and stop a slow rust problem you would otherwise be dealing with for years.

faqs.q: Is Maryborough or Hervey Bay easier to deliver into?
faqs.a: They are difficult in opposite ways. Hervey Bay blocks are level and tidy but tight, with narrow side setbacks that often force a crane lift over the fence. Maryborough has more room on many blocks but throws overhead obstacles at you: mature street trees with low canopies, deep kerbs and short steep driveways up to high-set houses. Industrial Maryborough is the easiest delivery in either town. The practical difference is that in Hervey Bay we ask about the side gap, and in Maryborough we ask what is above the truck.

faqs.q: What happens to a container when the Mary River comes up in Maryborough?
faqs.a: The same thing that happens to anything else at that level, which is why we will not tell you a container solves flooding. Water rising from below gets in at the door seals, and an empty unit will float and move once it is deep enough. What keeps contents dry is having the unit above where the water has historically reached on your block. On a property that has been through it, placement is the whole decision. Tell us how deep it got and where, and we will work out what the truck can reach that also puts the unit high enough.

faqs.q: Can a truck get into an older Maryborough street with big street trees?
faqs.a: Usually, but the answer depends on what is overhead rather than what is on the ground. A tilt-tray has to angle its deck to slide a container off, and that needs real vertical clearance, which a mature fig or poinciana over a narrow street does not always leave. Where the canopy is low, the options are a different truck, a lift from a clearer position, or a placement closer to the street. Have a look up before you ring us, and mention any low branches, because it changes which truck we send.

faqs.q: What size container suits an engineering or workshop yard?
faqs.a: A 20ft is the workhorse and it is what most yards start with, because it holds a serious amount of parts and tooling, fits into a corner of the hardstand and can still be lifted and moved when the layout changes. A 40ft makes sense where the storage is long items, racking runs or bulk consumables and the yard has the length to place it properly. Where the container will be moved between sites or stacked, the corner castings and the frame matter far more than paint, so spend the difference there.

locations.name: Gympie
locations.depot: Loaded at the Forest Hill yard and run north up the Bruce
locations.leadTime: Usually two to four business days
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft, which suits the short steep driveways here; side loader for 40ft on rural blocks with room
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Gympie. Steep driveways, Mary River flooding, forestry and rural blocks, with realistic delivery and placement advice.
locations.line: Gympie is the closest town on this list to our Forest Hill yard and one of the more interesting to deliver into. The trip is short. The last few hundred metres are frequently not. This is a town built across hills above a river that floods badly and often, and both of those facts shape where a container should go far more than the trucking does.
locations.uses: chainsaws, felling gear and machinery parts on the forestry and timber blocks, fencing, water fittings and feed on the small cattle and horse properties, tools and materials for the trades working across the region, storage lifted well above where the Mary has reached, machinery spares on the rural blocks out toward Kilkivan and Imbil, boat and fishing gear for people running to Tin Can Bay, and household storage during a build on an acreage block
access:
Gympie is hilly in a way that maps do not convey. The residential streets climb and drop sharply, driveways come off them at severe angles, and a good number of them turn hard within a few metres of the street. A tilt-tray unloading a container needs both a run of length and a reasonably consistent grade, and a driveway that pitches up steeply then breaks over a crest will ground the deck. That is the single most common reason a Gympie delivery needs rethinking, and it is entirely predictable from a photo.

Where the driveway will not work, the usual answers are a smaller unit, a placement closer to the street, or a lift from a position the truck can actually stand on. What does not work is optimism on the day, because a truck committed to a steep narrow driveway with a container on the back has very few options left.

Out of town the character changes completely. The rural and forestry country around Gympie has long entries, gates, grids and unsealed tracks, and the ground is generally decent where it is formed and unreliable where it is not. Timber country tracks are often steep, off-camber and cut into the side of a hill, with a soft outside edge that has never carried anything as heavy as a loaded rigid. Creek crossings on those tracks come up quickly in a wet spell and drop just as fast.

Rain is the recurring variable. The Mary catchment gets serious falls and the district goes from firm to unworkable in a day. We would rather move a Gympie date by forty-eight hours than put a truck somewhere it will cut ruts into a track you have to maintain.

sections.h: The town that floods, and the ground above it
p: Gympie floods more often and more severely than almost anywhere else in this part of the state, and the town has an unusually clear collective memory of exactly how high the water got and when. That local knowledge is more useful than any general advice we could give, so bring it to the conversation. What we will be straight about is what a container contributes. It keeps rain off from above and it locks. It does not resist rising water. Floodwater reaches the door seals and gets inside, and an empty unit will float and be moved by deep water.

The value here is entirely in placement. A container sitting above the level water has reached on your property keeps what is in it dry, and given the terrain in Gympie there is often somewhere on a block that is genuinely well above the risk. Working out where that is, and whether a truck can reach it, is the conversation worth having before ordering rather than after. Sometimes the good high spot is not truck-accessible and the answer becomes a smaller unit or a different approach, and it is better to know that early.

sections.h: Hills, hairpins and short steep driveways
p: The gradient problem in Gympie is not usually about power, it is about geometry. A tilt-tray needs to raise its deck to slide a container off, and it needs the ground behind it to be reasonably continuous while it does. A driveway that climbs hard from the street and then breaks over a crest, or one that turns sharply within a truck length of the road, does not offer that. The deck grounds, or the trailer cannot get square to the drop point, or there is no way to reverse back out afterwards.

There are good answers and they all start with knowing in advance. A 10ft or 20ft on a smaller truck manages a lot of these driveways that a 40ft could never attempt. A crane lift from the street works where there is somewhere to stand and nothing overhead. Placing the unit lower down the block and accepting a longer walk is sometimes simply the sensible trade. Send photos of the driveway from the street and from the top before you order, and we will tell you which of those it is.

sections.h: Timber country, small farms and gear that lives outdoors
p: The country around Gympie is a mix of forestry, small grazing blocks, horse properties and lifestyle acreage, and the storage need it produces is consistent: a lot of valuable equipment that currently lives under a tarp, in the back of a ute, or in a shed that ran out of room. Chainsaws and felling gear, fencing materials, water and irrigation fittings, feed, tack, tools and machinery parts. A container takes all of it off the ground and puts a lock on it, which is worth a great deal on a block that is empty during the day. The practical decisions that matter are where it sits and which way the doors face. On sloping ground the unit has to be properly levelled on bearers or pads under the corner castings, because a container out of level twists the frame and the doors start to bind within a season. Doors should face the way you will approach with a ute or a tractor, not the direction that happened to suit the delivery truck. Both are trivial to get right at placement and a genuine nuisance to fix afterwards.

faqs.q: The Mary River has been through my property. Is a container a sensible place for valuables?
faqs.a: It is a good lockup and it is dry from above, but it is not a defence against floodwater and we will not tell you it is. Water rising from below gets in at the door seals, and an empty container has enough buoyancy that deep water will lift and move it. What keeps contents dry is elevation, so the question is really where on your block the unit goes. Gympie's terrain often means there is a genuinely high spot available. Whether a truck can get to it is the next question, and one worth answering before you order.

faqs.q: My driveway is steep and turns sharply. Will that stop a delivery?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, but it decides the truck and possibly the size. A tilt-tray has to raise its deck to unload, and a driveway that climbs hard and then breaks over a crest, or turns within a truck length of the street, will ground the deck or leave no way to square up. A smaller unit on a smaller truck handles a lot of these. A lift from the street works where there is somewhere to stand and nothing overhead. Send us photos from the street and from the top and we will tell you which it is.

faqs.q: Is Gympie close enough to get a container out quickly?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is one of the shorter runs we do. Our yard is at Forest Hill in the Lockyer Valley and it is a straightforward trip north up the Bruce, so two to four business days is the normal window rather than the optimistic one. You are also close enough that coming to the yard to look at a unit before it is delivered is realistic if you want to, provided you ring first. If you would rather not make the trip, we can send photos of the actual unit on request before delivery.

faqs.q: Do containers get used on forestry and timber blocks around Gympie?
faqs.a: Regularly, and the reasons are straightforward. Felling and maintenance gear, chainsaws, fuel drums, chains and spare parts all need to be locked, dry and near where the work is, and the alternative is carting it back and forth or leaving it out. A container does that without an approval or a slab. On timber country the things to get right are the track in, because those are often steep with a soft outside edge, and levelling the unit properly on sloping ground so the doors keep closing after the first wet.
